clue.text: Loving proposal

blocks.note: first meaning: affectionate and gentle
second meaning: a formal offer, as in a bid for a contract

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a romantic proposal of marriage; the two words are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes gentle affection, and the noun is a formal offer submitted for consideration, such as a bid.

clue.text: Boring man promises to pay

blocks.note: Ted is a man's name
an IOU (I owe you) is a written promise to pay

explanation.surface: A dull man keeps writing out promises to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedious describes something long and dull, which is exactly what boring means.

clue.text: They smell good!

blocks.note: surface reading: some things have a pleasant scent
setter's reading: smell is an active verb, and these are good at doing it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Smell good' usually means giving off a nice odour; here it means being skilled at sniffing.
explanation.definitionFit: The facial organs used for detecting odours are what do the smelling, and do it well.

clue.text: Ron met Len Turner signing on

indicators.note: a turner turns things round, so the letters before it are spun into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter

explanation.surface: Ron met someone called Len Turner who was signing on for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner looks like Len's surname (or the painter); it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Enrolment is the act of officially joining a course or organisation, which is what signing on means.

clue.text: Fruit and nuts

blocks.note: first meaning: long yellow tropical fruits
second meaning: crazy, mad

explanation.walkthrough: Fruit and nuts sounds like a snack mix or chocolate bar; nuts here is the slang adjective for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the plural of a yellow tropical fruit and also informal slang meaning wildly crazy or mad.

clue.text: Drinks' dispenser

blocks.note: surface reading: a machine that dispenses drinks
setter's reading: a woman who serves drinks to customers in a pub

explanation.walkthrough: A dispenser suggests a machine; the setter means a person serving behind a pub counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman working behind a pub counter pours and hands out beer and spirits to customers.

clue.text: Called man back to meet editor

indicators.note: back means the word is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: taken as written
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: Someone phoned a man back to set up a meeting with an editor.
explanation.definitionFit: Named and called both mean given a particular name, as in a child called or named Tom.

clue.text: What people in prison call each other?

definitions.text: What people in prison call each other?

blocks.clueFragment: What people in prison call each other?
blocks.note: surface reading: the terms inmates use for one another

blocks.clueFragment: What people in prison call each other?
blocks.note: setter's reading: nick is British slang for prison, so a prison's names

explanation.walkthrough: Nick is British slang for a prison, so names used in the nick are, punningly, informal names.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal or affectionate substitute names given to people, such as Shorty, are what friends use among themselves.

clue.text: Skinhead to pass youth leader a drink

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: read as skin's head: the first letter of skin
to hand something is to pass it
the initial letter

explanation.surface: A skinhead hands a young gang leader a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skinhead' must be split into Skin and head. A shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, a British pub staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A shandy is a drink of beer diluted with lemonade or ginger beer.

clue.text: Relief road close to canyon

blocks.note: by means near or close to
a pass is a gap through mountains, like a canyon

explanation.surface: A new road to ease traffic runs near a canyon.
explanation.definitionFit: A bypass is a road that goes round a town to relieve congestion, which British planners call a relief road.

clue.text: Upset, yet orders vessel

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the following letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed yet keeps ordering a ship around.
explanation.definitionFit: A destroyer is a fast warship, and a warship is a kind of naval vessel.

clue.text: Caught accountant following me to the Holy City

indicators.note: following tells us the later pieces come after the word placed first

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
CA is a chartered accountant

explanation.surface: A cricketer and an accountant tag along behind me on a pilgrimage.
explanation.definitionFit: Mecca in Saudi Arabia is Islam's holiest city, the destination of the hajj pilgrimage.

clue.text: Bird in house left to die

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows

blocks.note: found spanning the two words, after the opening h

explanation.surface: A bird trapped in a house has been abandoned to its death.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing 'to die' only completes the picture and gives no letters. An ousel (or ouzel) is an old name for the blackbird, also used of the ring ouzel and dipper.
explanation.definitionFit: An ousel is a thrush-family songbird, the traditional name for the blackbird and related species.

clue.text: Deserted Group 1 in time

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the word that follows

blocks.note: AD, anno domini, marks a period of time in dates
a band is a group of musicians
the numeral written as a word

explanation.surface: A pop act called Group 1 has been left high and dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Abandoned means left empty or forsaken, as a deserted village is one its people have left behind.

clue.text: One won't be happy to show it

definitions.text: One won't be happy to show it

blocks.clueFragment: One won't be happy to show it
blocks.note: surface reading: someone reluctant to display something

blocks.clueFragment: One won't be happy to show it
blocks.note: setter's reading: the thing displayed is the very feeling of not being happy

explanation.surface: Someone is reluctant to put something on show.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'won't be happy to' as unwilling; the setter means a person displaying this is literally not happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorrow is the opposite of happiness, so anyone displaying sorrow is by definition unhappy.

clue.text: Change ends ideal time limits

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the letters that follow into another order

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter

explanation.surface: Altering how things finish makes for the perfect schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadlines are fixed points by which tasks must be finished, so they set limits in time.

clue.text: Last month a politician wanted to abscond

blocks.note: December is the final month of the year, abbreviated
taken as written
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician tried to run off with the money last month.
explanation.definitionFit: To decamp is to leave suddenly or secretly, which is exactly what absconding involves.

clue.text: Something to scoff at?

blocks.note: surface reading: an object of mockery or derision
setter's reading: scoff is British slang for eat greedily, so a place to eat at

explanation.walkthrough: To scoff at is to mock, but in British slang to scoff is to wolf down food, so this is a place for eating.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-service restaurant, often in a workplace or college, is where people go to eat meals.

clue.text: Drink one brought in by restaurant employee

indicators.note: brought in means one piece is carried inside another

blocks.note: water is a drink
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A drink is carried to the table by the restaurant staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A waiter serves food and drink to diners, a member of staff working in a restaurant.

clue.text: He leaves here, failing to slip back

indicators.note: leaves means one part departs from the word, removing those letters

blocks.note: taken as written, to be removed
taken as written
a lapse is a failing or slip

explanation.surface: A man walks out of here, unable to sneak back in.
explanation.definitionFit: To relapse is to fall back into a previous worse state, such as illness or bad habits.

clue.text: Declined to postpone backing American intervention

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is read in reverse
an intervention steps in between, so one piece goes into the middle of another

blocks.note: to defer is to put off
US is the standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Someone said no to delaying a project that had American backing.
explanation.definitionFit: Refused and declined both mean said no to an offer or request, a straightforward synonym pair.

clue.text: Army regiment kind to holiday centre

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
a sort is a kind or type

explanation.surface: An army regiment is kind enough to visit a holiday camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort is a place people visit for holidays and recreation, such as a seaside town.

clue.text: Place of confinement none dug out of

indicators.note: out of here means formed from a jumble of the letters given

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter

explanation.surface: A prison cell no one has ever tunnelled out of.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is a dark underground prison cell, typically beneath a castle, where captives were held.

clue.text: Strolled in the morning, then gave blood

blocks.note: am, ante meridiem, means before noon
to bleed is to lose or give blood

explanation.surface: Someone took a morning walk and then went to donate blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambled means walked at a slow, relaxed pace, the same leisurely gait as strolled.

clue.text: Mounds of earth first made by Shell Oil, perhaps

indicators.note: first picks out only the opening letter of the next word
perhaps hints the letters are only a possible arrangement, to be reworked

blocks.note: the initial letter of this word
the fodder, every letter

explanation.surface: An oil company digging for oil throws up heaps of soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Molehills are small heaps of soil pushed up by burrowing moles, so they are mounds of earth.

clue.text: He returned Ann's flowering shrub

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the following name runs in reverse

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man gives back a woman's plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's just joins Ann to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Henna is a tropical flowering shrub whose leaves yield a reddish dye for hair and skin.

clue.text: Coach coaches

blocks.note: first meaning: as a verb, to instruct or prepare someone
second meaning: as a noun, a line of railway carriages

explanation.walkthrough: The first word is a verb, to teach; the second is a noun, railway carriages, collectively one connected vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: To train someone is to instruct them; a train is a connected series of railway carriages pulled together.

clue.text: Some said education helped

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the following words is used

blocks.note: found across the two words, from the a of said

explanation.surface: Someone claimed that schooling had been beneficial.
explanation.definitionFit: Aided and helped are straightforward synonyms, both meaning gave assistance to someone.

clue.text: Product name for sheets, perhaps

blocks.note: a product line is a range of goods
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A shop gives a brand name to its range of bed sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks sheets as one example of the answer; household linen also covers towels and tablecloths.
explanation.definitionFit: Bed sheets are one kind of household textile that traditionally goes by this collective name.

clue.text: Bird with separate crest

blocks.note: to part is to separate
a crest is the top line of a hill

explanation.surface: A bird sports a distinctive crest on its head.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'crest' a bird's head feathers and 'separate' an adjective; really separate is a verb and crest a hilltop.
explanation.definitionFit: The partridge is a plump game bird of fields and farmland, hunted in shooting season.

clue.text: See AIDS as an illness

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter

explanation.surface: A public message urges people to regard AIDS as a serious illness.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal; the setter relies on 'See' and the neat surface, so the solver must notice the seven letters fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease is a disorder of body or mind with recognisable symptoms, in other words a sickness.

clue.text: Girl has to help men out

indicators.note: out suggests letters turned out of their places and rearranged

blocks.note: aid means help
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl must lend a hand to some men in difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Maiden is an old-fashioned or poetic word for a young unmarried woman or girl.
